John Cage, born in 1912 and died in 1992, was an American composer, music theorist, philosopher, and artist who was a leading figure of the post-war avant-garde. A pioneer of indeterminacy in music, electroacoustic music, and non-standard instrument usage, Cage questioned the fundamental boundaries of art and music.

His most famous and controversial work is four minutes thirty-three seconds, written in 1952. This is a three-movement piece in which the performer or performers remain completely silent, and the music consists of the ambient sounds of the environment and the audience during the performance. Cage invented the prepared piano technique in 1940, inserting screws, bolts, rubber bands, and felt between the strings of a grand piano to alter its pitch, timbre, and resonance, creating a gamelan-like percussive sound. Sonatas and Interludes from nineteen forty-six to nineteen forty-eight is a landmark cycle of sixteen sonatas and four interludes for prepared piano, designed to express the nine rasas, or permanent emotions, of Indian aesthetic theory. Music of Changes from 1951 is a piece for solo piano that pioneered aleatoric, or chance-based, composition, in which Cage used the I Ching, the ancient Chinese Book of Changes, to determine all parameters of pitch, duration, and dynamics. As Slow as Possible, an organ piece from 1987, has an ongoing performance at a church in Halberstadt, Germany that began in 2001 and is scheduled to last six hundred thirty-nine years, making it the longest musical performance in history.

Black Mountain College was the experimental North Carolina arts school where Cage staged Theater Piece No. 1 in 1952, a multi-media event widely regarded as the first artistic happening. He was a revolutionary figure who redefined the parameters of American experimental music. Cage studied composition under Arnold Schoenberg in Los Angeles, and Schoenberg famously described Cage not as a composer, but as an inventor of genius.
